items.source: Bespoke Investment Group (Substack)
items.title: Waller's July 13 speech scores among the most hawkish Fed remarks since 1994
items.idea: Bespoke runs 8 separate NLP models (dictionary-based, rate-cycle regression, market-reaction regression) against every FOMC statement, minutes, Beige Book and speech since 1994. Governor Waller's July 13 speech scored in the top percentile for hawkishness on the two dictionary-based measures — only a handful of Fed communications in 30+ years scored higher. Waller has historically been an early mover ahead of full-committee consensus.
items.angle: If Waller — a governor who typically leads shifts in Fed thinking before the committee follows — is scoring near-record hawkish on an objective NLP measure, the hike repricing has real institutional backing, not just market noise. Relevant to rate-sensitive positioning: TLT, financials, gold.
items.tweetA: Bespoke ran 8 NLP models on every Fed speech since 1994. Waller's July 13 remarks land in the top percentile for hawkishness in three decades. He's usually the guy who moves before the committee does. The market is still debating cuts vs hikes — Waller already answered.
items.tweetB: Everyone's arguing about whether the Fed cuts or holds. Bespoke's hawk/dove NLP score says that's the wrong question — Waller's speech scored more hawkish than all but a handful of Fed communications since 1994. The next FOMC surprise is a hike, not a cut.

charts.desc: Bar chart comparing 8 hawk/dove scoring methods for Waller's speech, plus a chart of historical hawkish/dovish percentile scores for all Fed communications since 1994 — Waller's speech sits near the very top.

items.source: Blind Squirrel Macro / 'Arcadia' (Substack)
items.title: A 1990s Turkish bank IPO killed by hyperinflation accounting is still the lesson for 2026 Turkey bulls
items.idea: Author recounts prepping a Turkish bank IPO in the mid-1990s that died at the finish line once IAS 29 hyperinflation-accounting adjustments were applied — the local-GAAP ROE that looked attractive collapsed into 'a minnow with an adjusted ROE barely perceptible to the naked eye' once restated for ~70% CPI. Thirty years later, the author argues 2026 Turkey is still 'Europe geography, Asia growth' trading at a persistent discount for the same reason.
items.angle: Turkish equities screen cheap nominally, but the discount exists precisely because every cycle an investor has to underwrite the CPI/IAS 29 haircut before trusting the multiple. Relevant for anyone eyeing Turkish banks or $TUR as a value trade right now.
items.tweetA: 1990s lesson relearned: a Turkish bank IPO died because IAS 29 hyperinflation accounting turned an attractive local-GAAP ROE into a rounding error. Thirty years later, Turkish equities still screen 'cheap' in nominal terms. Inflation-adjust before you buy the multiple.
items.tweetB: The Turkey pitch never changes: 'Europe geography, Asia growth, discount valuation.' What also never changes: the discount exists because CPI inflation eats the equity story every single cycle. $TUR bulls — have you actually run the IAS 29 math, or just the headline P/E?

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom (Substack) — Forex Weekly
items.title: DXY is flat, but that's cancellation, not calm — the real move is in the crosses
items.idea: Despite a ~40% July surge in oil, a hawkish Fed pivot and elevated geopolitical risk, the Dollar index has stayed 'stubbornly contained.' The author frames this as 'resilience without momentum': the index is masking a split market where high-carry, commodity-linked currencies are outperforming while low-yield, energy-importer currencies are being sold — the index just averages the two moves to flat.
items.angle: Trading DXY itself is dead money right now; the alpha is in the cross-currency dispersion (long commodity FX vs short funding-currency FX), not in the index direction.
items.tweetA: DXY hasn't moved. That's not calm, it's cancellation. Commodity-linked, high-carry currencies are ripping while energy-importer, low-yield currencies get dumped, and the index just averages it all out to flat. The trade isn't the Dollar direction — it's the dispersion hiding inside it.
items.tweetB: Oil +40% in July, the Fed talking hikes again, geopolitical risk elevated — and the Dollar index barely blinked. If a shock this size can't move DXY, the index has stopped being the story this quarter. Watch the crosses, not the headline number.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom (Substack) — Forex Weekly
items.title: The Euro has stopped being a destination currency and become the market's preferred funding leg
items.idea: EUR/USD now trades almost purely as Dollar-beta because the Eurozone imports energy and offers no independent carry story — every euro spent on higher gas prices is a euro not spent on domestic demand or the currency. German fiscal stimulus is being drowned out by the worsening energy terms of trade. The author says the Euro is 'increasingly useful as a funding leg' for carry trades rather than something traders want to own outright.
items.angle: EUR weakness right now isn't a EUR-specific bear call, it's a byproduct of the market using it to fund longs elsewhere — the structural short bias persists as long as gas prices stay elevated, regardless of the ECB's next move.
items.tweetA: The Euro isn't being sold because anyone hates Europe. It's being sold because it's now the cheapest, most liquid way to fund a long-carry trade — no domestic yield edge, worsening energy terms of trade. A currency becomes a funding leg exactly when nobody wants to own it outright.
items.tweetB: German fiscal stimulus was supposed to be this year's Euro bull case. It's being drowned out by the energy import bill instead. Every dollar spent on gas is a dollar not spent on domestic demand — or the currency. $EURUSD structurally capped until gas rolls over.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom (Substack) — Forex Weekly
items.title: Sterling's July honeymoon is ending as markets start pricing who pays for new UK spending
items.idea: Sterling rallied in July on political optimism and attractive carry, but that grace period is fading as markets test the funding arithmetic behind new government spending ahead of the Autumn Budget. UK rate markets are already priced well past the Bank of England's on-hold baseline — if growth softens, hike bets could unwind even as the fiscal risk premium rises.
items.angle: Classic 'buy the rumor, sell the fiscal reality' setup — GBP looks asymmetrically vulnerable into Autumn Budget headlines even without a full-blown gilt-crisis scenario.
items.tweetA: Sterling's July honeymoon is over — not because of a crisis, just arithmetic. New spending pledges are being tested against 'who pays for this' before the Autumn Budget even lands. Fiscal premia don't arrive with a headline; they show up in the gilt curve first, then the currency.
items.tweetB: UK rate markets are priced further into hikes than the BoE's own guidance supports. If growth softens, that's not a Sterling-bullish setup — it's a scenario where hike bets unwind AND the fiscal risk premium rises at the same time. $GBPUSD asymmetry points down into autumn.

items.title: Speculative short-Yen positioning is back at 2024 carry-unwind levels — but the macro fuel is different this time

items.angle: This is a positioning trade, not a macro trade. The setup — 'everyone already owns this' — historically doesn't need a full macro reversal to unwind painfully.
items.tweetA: USD/JPY short-Yen positioning is back at 2024 carry-unwind levels. The difference: in 2024 the unwind was fueled by falling US yields and recession fear. Today the macro backdrop is the opposite — Fed talking hikes, not cuts. Same crowding, different fuel source. That's what makes this setup worth watching closely, not fading blind.
items.tweetB: The scariest setup in FX right now isn't a macro call, it's a crowd call: everyone is short Yen at 40-year highs. It doesn't need a regime change to snap — just one soft US yield print or a hint of Japanese capital repatriation. This is positioning risk, not fundamentals risk.

items.angle: A clean case of a macro narrative (rate divergence) losing to a physical-market variable (energy shock) — a reminder that not every FX cross is currently trading on rate differentials, even when the rate story looks compelling on paper.
items.tweetA: New Zealand just printed a hot CPI surprise that should send AUD/NZD lower on rate convergence. It hasn't moved, because Australia's commodity-exporter status is currently a bigger factor than either country's central bank. Oil is overriding rate differentials in FX crosses right now — not just in energy names.
items.tweetB: AUD/NZD is the cleanest example of the energy shock hijacking FX macro this month: New Zealand's inflation surprise should be bearish the cross, but Australia's terms-of-trade windfall from higher oil is fully offsetting it. Central bank divergence isn't driving this pair — commodities are.

items.title: 'The one thing you can't buy in a store is the euphoria of peril' — a 1923 mining tycoon's pitch for 2026 markets
items.idea: Via a scene from the Yellowstone prequel '1923,' the newsletter frames modern consumer capitalism as literally packaging manufactured danger for people who already have everything — the villain's line: 'It's a rich man's world now, and everyone gets a taste... the one thing you can't buy in a store is the euphoria of peril, the exhilaration of danger. I can sell that. For a fortune.'
items.angle: Maps directly onto observable trends: prediction markets, 0DTE options, leveraged perpetuals and meme-coin speculation are all monetizing manufactured danger for a bored, comfortable retail base — worth connecting to retail options volume and gambling-adjacent fintech growth as a genuine secular demand driver, not just 'retail is dumb.'
items.tweetA: A 1923 mining tycoon's line nails 2026 retail markets: 'It's a rich man's world now, and everyone gets a taste — the one thing you can't buy in a store is the euphoria of peril. I can sell that for a fortune.' That's 0DTE options, prediction markets, and meme coins in a single sentence.
items.tweetB: Scarcity used to be about goods. Now it's about danger — that's the actual product being sold by prediction markets, leveraged perpetuals and 0DTE options. Nobody's buying the payout distribution. They're buying the adrenaline. Price it accordingly if you understand the real demand curve.

items.idea: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang made his personal debut on X with a letter arguing that open-weight AI models are essential for safety, innovation and 'sovereignty' — positioned alongside, not instead of, closed frontier labs.
items.angle: Nvidia's business model benefits from a fragmented, multi-model world where dozens of players buy GPUs rather than a handful of closed labs consolidating compute demand and negotiating leverage. Huang publicly championing open models reads as Nvidia hedging against exactly that consolidation.
items.tweetA: Jensen Huang's first-ever personal X post isn't a product announcement — it's a policy argument for open models on safety and 'sovereignty' grounds. Notice who benefits from a fragmented AI landscape with dozens of model builders instead of three closed labs: the company selling the chips to all of them.
items.tweetB: Read between the lines: Nvidia doesn't care who wins the model war, it cares how many players are still buying GPUs when it's over. Huang debuting on X to champion open AI is Nvidia hedging against demand concentration in 2-3 closed labs. $NVDA

items.source: Salazar Slytherin / Crypto Integrated (Substack) — Crypto News
items.title: BitMEX — the exchange that pioneered perpetual futures — and DEX Dango both announced shutdowns in the same week
items.idea: BitMEX (founded 2014, widely credited with inventing the crypto perpetual futures contract) announced it will shut down operations effective September 23, 2026. Separately, DEX Dango announced it is winding down effective August 13. Two very different eras and business models of crypto infrastructure closing within days of each other.
items.angle: Two very different crypto-infra generations (a legacy derivatives pioneer and a newer DEX) closing shop the same week that Fidelity and Samsung push further into stablecoin adoption is a live data point on how much competitive/regulatory pressure is squeezing exchange economics even during a headline-strong institutional-adoption cycle.
items.tweetA: BitMEX — the exchange that arguably invented the perpetual futures contract in 2014 — is shutting down the same week as newer DEX Dango. Different business models, same week, same outcome. Crypto exchange economics are getting squeezed even while institutional adoption headlines (Fidelity, Samsung) are accelerating.
items.tweetB: Bifurcation happening in real time: legacy exchanges (BitMEX) and smaller DEXs (Dango) are closing shop the same week Fidelity launches a stablecoin and Samsung ships wallet support to hundreds of millions of phones. The winners and losers of crypto's institutionalization are being sorted out live.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom (Substack) — Three Crosscurrents
items.title: JPM's own oil model shows the market pricing a Hormuz resolution that the tanker data doesn't support yet
items.idea: JPMorgan estimates Brent near $100 contains only a ~$13/bbl geopolitical premium, despite Strait of Hormuz tanker traffic sitting near 50% of pre-war levels — well below the ~73% recovery JPM's own base case assumes. Their framework: disruption contained to 1 month → Brent ~$94; each additional month adds $7-8/bbl; 3 months → ~$114; each extra 1mbpd of Chinese crude imports adds ~$3/bbl. Gasoline could move from ~$4.20 (1 month) to above $4.50 (2 months) — historically the level where economic discomfort becomes political pain.
items.angle: The market's pricing a fast resolution (~$13 premium) despite tanker-traffic data showing the disruption running well below the recovery already baked into that low premium — the risk/reward on oil-linked longs looks asymmetric if disruption simply persists at the current run-rate, let alone escalates further.
items.tweetA: JPMorgan says Brent's geopolitical premium is only $13/bbl right now. But Hormuz tanker traffic is stuck near 50% of pre-war levels — well below the 73% the bank is assuming recovers in its own base case. The oil market is pricing a resolution the actual tanker data isn't showing yet. $USO $XLE
items.tweetB: Do the math JPM laid out: every extra month of Hormuz disruption adds $7-8/bbl to fair value. We're not at month one anymore. Drag this to month three and that's $114 Brent and $4.50+ gasoline — the exact level where 'economic discomfort becomes political pain.' That's the actual catalyst to watch, not the next headline.

items.title: Meta's AI bonds went from par to 109 to 97 — the bond market is repricing AI credit faster than equity headlines suggest
items.idea: Meta's $27.3B Hyperion data-center financing was issued at par, traded up to 109, then fell back to 97. Separately, Alphabet raised 2026 capex guidance to $195-205B, reported negative $5.9B quarterly free cash flow despite 82% cloud growth, and the stock still fell 6.9%. Goldman notes investment-grade corporate issuance is starting to outpace Treasury issuance, driven in part by record hyperscaler AI borrowing.
items.angle: The market's scoring system flipped: a year ago more capex signaled ambition; now the same guidance raise reads as 'the bill is arriving faster than the revenue.' Each hyperscaler's capex hike forces competitors to match it — a financing arms race, not just a technology one. Meta's bond round-trip (par→109→97) is a cleaner real-time gauge of AI credit sentiment than equity multiples.
items.tweetA: Meta's $27.3B Hyperion AI bonds went from par, to 109, to 97. That round trip is the actual price of AI-infrastructure credit risk right now — and it moved more than most people's read on AI sentiment from equity headlines alone. Watch the bond, not the stock, for the real repricing.
items.tweetB: Alphabet grew cloud 82%, raised capex guidance to $205B, burned $5.9B of free cash flow in a single quarter — and the stock fell 6.9%. A year ago that capex raise would've been read as conviction. Now it's read as 'the bill beat the revenue.' The market's AI scoring system just flipped, and nobody's repriced Meta or Amazon for it yet. $META $AMZN
